title: Separating Mixtures
description: Techniques for separating mixtures — filtration, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, and choosing the right method.

notes.heading: Pure Substances vs Mixtures
notes.body: A pure substance consists of only ONE type of element or compound. It has a fixed, sharp melting point and boiling point. Examples: pure water (H₂O), pure gold, pure sodium chloride. A mixture contains two or more different substances NOT chemically combined — they can be separated by physical methods. Mixtures melt/boil over a range of temperatures (not a sharp point). Examples: air (mixture of N₂, O₂, CO₂), seawater (water + salt), crude oil (mixture of hydrocarbons). In a mixture, each substance retains its own properties. The composition of a mixture can vary, unlike a pure compound which has a fixed composition. Important: dissolving is a physical change, not chemical — when salt dissolves in water, you can recover the salt by evaporation; the salt is still NaCl.

notes.heading: Filtration and Evaporation
notes.body: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel. The liquid (filtrate) passes through; the insoluble solid (residue) stays on the paper. Examples: separating sand from water, collecting a precipitate after a reaction. Filter paper has tiny pores that allow liquid molecules through but trap larger solid particles. Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid. The solution is heated in an evaporating dish. The liquid (solvent) evaporates, leaving the solid (solute) behind. This works because the solvent has a lower boiling point than the solute. Example: obtaining salt from seawater. Limitation: evaporation does NOT collect the solvent — it is lost to the air. For collecting both solute AND solvent, use distillation or crystallisation.

notes.heading: Crystallisation
notes.body: Crystallisation separates a soluble solid from a solution while preserving the solvent AND producing pure, well-formed crystals. Method: (1) Gently heat the solution to evaporate some solvent until the solution is saturated (crystals begin to form at the edge — 'crystallisation point'). (2) Stop heating and allow to cool slowly. (3) As the solution cools, solubility decreases and pure crystals form. (4) Filter the crystals, wash with cold distilled water (removes impurities), and dry between filter paper or in a warm oven. Slow cooling produces larger, purer crystals because molecules have time to arrange properly. Rapid cooling traps impurities. Crystallisation is preferred over evaporation when: you want pure crystals (evaporation can trap impurities), the solid decomposes on heating, or you want well-defined crystals for analysis.

notes.heading: Simple and Fractional Distillation
notes.body: Distillation separates a liquid from a solution OR separates two miscible liquids with different boiling points. Simple distillation: (1) The mixture is heated in a flask. (2) The substance with the lower boiling point vaporises first. (3) Vapour passes into a condenser (water jacket — cold water in at bottom, out at top). (4) Vapour cools and condenses back to liquid — the distillate is collected. Example: obtaining pure water from salt water. The salt stays in the flask. Fractional distillation separates two or more miscible liquids with similar boiling points (e.g., ethanol (78°C) and water (100°C)). A fractionating column filled with glass beads or packed material provides a large surface area. Vapours rise, condense on the beads, and re-evaporate — this repeated condensation/vaporisation enriches the vapour in the more volatile component. The column temperature decreases from bottom to top. The liquid with the lower boiling point reaches the top and is collected first. Applications: separating crude oil into fractions (petrol, diesel, etc.), producing distilled spirits (ethanol from fermented mixture).

notes.heading: Paper Chromatography
notes.body: Chromatography separates dissolved substances based on their different solubilities and attractions to a stationary phase. In paper chromatography: (1) A small spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil baseline (NEVER pen — ink would dissolve and run) near the bottom of chromatography paper. (2) The paper is suspended so the bottom edge just touches the solvent (water or organic solvent) — the baseline must be ABOVE the solvent level. (3) The solvent travels up the paper by capillary action (the mobile phase). (4) Different substances travel at different rates depending on their solubility in the solvent and their attraction to the paper (stationary phase). (5) The result is a chromatogram — a series of spots at different heights. The Rf (retention factor) value identifies a substance: Rf = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent front. Rf is always between 0 and 1. Each substance has a characteristic Rf for a given solvent and paper type. Uses: identifying food dyes, analysing inks in forgery cases, separating chlorophyll pigments, drug testing.

notes.heading: Magnetism, Decanting, and Other Methods
notes.body: Magnetic separation: uses a magnet to remove magnetic materials (iron, cobalt, nickel) from non-magnetic mixtures. Example: separating iron filings from sulfur powder in a recycling plant. Decanting: carefully pouring off a liquid from a settled solid (sediment). Quick but imprecise — leaves some liquid behind. Example: pouring clear water off settled mud. Separating funnel: separates immiscible liquids (that do not mix) based on density. The mixture forms two layers; the denser liquid is drained through the tap at the bottom. Example: separating oil from water. The key principle for ALL separation techniques: exploit a difference in physical properties — particle size (filtration), boiling point (distillation), solubility (crystallisation, chromatography), density (separating funnel), or magnetism.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Separation Technique
notes.body: How to decide: (1) Identify what you are separating — solids from liquids? Two liquids? Dissolved solids? (2) Identify the relevant physical property difference. Decision flowchart: Insoluble solid + liquid → Filtration. Soluble solid dissolved in liquid → Crystallisation (keep both) OR Evaporation (only need solid). Liquid from a solution → Simple distillation. Two miscible liquids → Fractional distillation. Coloured dissolved substances → Chromatography. Magnetic solid + non-magnetic solid → Magnet. Two immiscible liquids → Separating funnel. Common exam scenarios: (a) Pure water from salt water → Simple distillation (collects water, leaves salt). (b) Pure salt from salt water → Crystallisation (or evaporation). (c) Sand + salt mixture → (i) Add water to dissolve salt, (ii) Filter — sand residue, salt filtrate, (iii) Crystallise/evaporate filtrate to get salt. (d) Identify dyes in a sweet → Chromatography. (e) Ethanol + water mixture → Fractional distillation.

flashcards.definition: A single element or compound with a fixed, sharp melting/boiling point. Not mixed with anything else.
flashcards.example: Pure water boils at exactly 100°C; salt water boils over a range.

flashcards.definition: Separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Filtrate passes through filter paper; residue stays.
flashcards.example: Separating sand from water: sand stays on filter paper; clear water passes through.

flashcards.definition: Separating a soluble solid by evaporating solvent until saturated, then cooling to form pure crystals.
flashcards.example: Obtaining pure copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution.

flashcards.definition: Separates a liquid from a solution: heat → vapour → condense → pure distillate. Solute remains.
flashcards.example: Getting pure water from salt water: water boils at 100°C → vapour → condenses → pure water collected.

flashcards.definition: Separates miscible liquids with different boiling points using a fractionating column for repeated condensation/vaporisation.
flashcards.example: Separating ethanol (78°C) from water (100°C). Crude oil fractions: petrol, diesel, bitumen.

flashcards.definition: Separates dissolved substances based on differential solubility and attraction to stationary phase. Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent front.
flashcards.example: Analysing food colouring — different dyes travel different distances up paper.

flashcards.definition: Retention factor: distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Identifies a substance (0-1).
flashcards.example: A dye spot moved 4 cm; solvent front moved 10 cm. Rf = 0.4.

flashcards.definition: The liquid that passes through filter paper during filtration — contains dissolved substances.
flashcards.example: In sand + salt water filtration, the filtrate is the clear salt solution.

flashcards.definition: The solid left behind on filter paper after filtration.
flashcards.example: After filtering sand + water, the residue is wet sand on the filter paper.

flashcards.definition: Miscible liquids mix completely (e.g., ethanol + water). Immiscible liquids do NOT mix and form layers (e.g., oil + water).
flashcards.example: Oil and water are immiscible — they form two layers and can be separated using a separating funnel.

flashcards.definition: The solvent that moves through the stationary phase, carrying dissolved substances with it at different rates.
flashcards.example: In paper chromatography, the mobile phase is the solvent (water or ethanol) travelling up the paper.

flashcards.definition: The fixed material through which the mobile phase travels. Substances interact with it differently, affecting separation.
flashcards.example: In paper chromatography, the cellulose paper is the stationary phase.

questions.stem: Which technique separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
questions.explanation: Filtration uses filter paper — liquid passes through, insoluble solid stays as residue.

questions.stem: How would you obtain pure water from salt water?
choices: Simple distillation — water boils, vapour condenses, pure water collected; salt remains
questions.explanation: Simple distillation collects pure water as distillate. Filtration wouldn't work (salt is dissolved, not insoluble). Evaporation would lose the water.

questions.stem: A spot moved 3 cm; solvent front moved 12 cm. Rf = ?
Why must the baseline be drawn in pencil, not pen, in chromatography?
choices: Pen ink would dissolve in the solvent and run, contaminating the chromatogram
Pencil shows up better on paper
questions.explanation: Pen ink is itself a mixture of dyes that would dissolve and separate, interfering with the results. Pencil (graphite) is insoluble.

choices: Fractional distillation — boiling points are different but both evaporate; fractionating column achieves separation
questions.explanation: Both are liquids with close boiling points. Fractional distillation provides repeated condensation/vaporisation cycles to separate them cleanly.

questions.stem: Why does slow cooling produce larger crystals in crystallisation?
choices: Molecules have more time to arrange in an ordered crystal lattice before being frozen in place
Temperature does not affect crystal size
questions.explanation: Slow cooling gives particles time to find the lowest-energy positions in the growing crystal lattice → larger, more ordered crystals. Rapid cooling traps particles randomly → small, impure crystals.

questions.stem: Oil and water are immiscible. Which apparatus separates them?
choices: Separating funnel — oil (less dense) floats on water; drain water from bottom
questions.explanation: A separating funnel separates immiscible liquids by density. Water (denser) is drained through the tap; oil remains.

questions.stem: To separate sand, salt, and iron filings from a mixture:
choices: Add water, filter, then evaporate — sand stays on filter, salt dissolves; use magnet for iron
Use magnet → iron removed. Add water → salt dissolves. Filter → sand residue. Evaporate filtrate → salt crystals
questions.explanation: Step 1: Magnet removes iron. Step 2: Add water to dissolve salt. Step 3: Filter — sand stays. Step 4: Evaporate/crystallise filtrate → salt.

questions.stem: In simple distillation, why does cold water enter the condenser at the BOTTOM?
choices: It doesn't — cold water enters at the top
To ensure the condenser is completely filled with cold water (counter-current flow) for maximum cooling efficiency
It's easier to connect tubing that way
questions.explanation: Water enters at the bottom and exits at the top. This counter-current flow ensures the coolest water meets the vapour at the point where it's about to exit, maximising condensation.

questions.stem: Two substances have the same Rf value in a given solvent. What does this suggest?
choices: They may be the same substance — further testing with different solvents is needed
Rf values cannot be the same
questions.explanation: Same Rf suggests they COULD be the same, but confirmation requires running the chromatography again with a different solvent — different substances can coincidentally have the same Rf in one solvent.

questions.stem: Why is the baseline placed ABOVE the solvent level in chromatography?
choices: To make it easier to see
If the baseline is submerged, the sample spots would dissolve directly into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper
Solvent cannot travel above the baseline
questions.explanation: If the spots are in the solvent, they dissolve and mix into the bulk solvent — no separation occurs. The spots must be above the solvent so the mobile phase carries them upwards.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of evaporation compared to crystallisation?
choices: The solvent is lost to the air and the solid may be impure or decompose if overheated
questions.explanation: Evaporation loses the solvent and can trap impurities in the solid crust. If heated too strongly, some solids decompose thermally. Crystallisation preserves purity and solvent.

questions.stem: A pure substance has a melting point of 122-123°C. An impure sample will:
choices: Melt over a wider range and at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice → lower melting point and broader melting range.

questions.stem: Which properties does fractional distillation exploit to separate crude oil?
choices: Different boiling points of hydrocarbon fractions
questions.explanation: Crude oil is separated into fractions (petrol, kerosene, diesel, bitumen) based on boiling point ranges in a fractionating tower.

questions.stem: A chromatogram shows three spots from a sample and one spot from a known dye at the same height. What conclusion?
choices: One component of the sample matches the known dye (same Rf value)
All spots are the same substance
questions.explanation: A spot at the same height (same Rf) suggests one component is the known dye. The other spots are different substances in the mixture.
